bai.moTa: What free fall cannot remove: tidal forces
bai.yChinh: Free fall can remove gravity at one place, but it cannot remove the **difference** in gravity between two nearby places: the tidal force. A cloud of freely falling particles gets stretched along the radial direction and squeezed in the two sideways directions. That is the **curvature** of spacetime. Einstein’s equation says: where there is matter, the volume of such a cloud starts to shrink with an acceleration proportional to the energy density plus three times the pressure.
bai.conSo.1: **1.1 × 10⁻⁶ m/s²**: the tidal acceleration of the Moon at Earth’s surface.
bai.conSo.2: **2.6 × 10⁻⁶ m/s² per meter**: the tidal stretch aboard the International Space Station.
bai.conSo.3: **2 × 10⁸ m/s²**: the difference between the head and feet of a 2 m tall person at the horizon of a 10-solar-mass black hole; for Sgr A* only about 10⁻³ m/s².
bai.conSo.4: **10**: the number of component equations in Einstein’s equation (each side is a symmetric 4 × 4 table).
bai.hieuDung: **Free fall does not remove all of gravity.** It removes only the uniform part at one place. The tidal force (the difference in gravity between two nearby places) cannot be removed by any frame; that is the true curvature of spacetime. The model uses Newtonian mechanics, which is correct in weak fields up to errors of order GM/(rc²); in tide mode the water bulges are exaggerated about 2 million times.
bai.nguon: Einstein’s equation stated in terms of volume: Baez and Bunn 2005, Am. J. Phys. 73, 644. Curvature, geodesic deviation and Einstein’s equation: Hartle 2003, ch. 21. Constants: Moon’s GM 4.9028 × 10¹² m³/s², Earth’s GM 3.986004418 × 10¹⁴ m³/s², Sun’s GM 1.32712440018 × 10²⁰ m³/s² (JPL); mean Earth–Moon distance 384,400 km; Sgr A* 4.3 million solar masses (GRAVITY). Particle cloud simulation: Newtonian mechanics, velocity Verlet.

bai.baiGiang.buoc.1.ten: Free fall removes gravity, but not all of it
bai.baiGiang.buoc.1.noiDung:
A cloud of small particles, at rest relative to one another, is released to fall toward a planet. In Lesson 7 and Lesson 8 we saw that someone in {{rơi tự do|free fall}} along with the cloud feels no gravity: all the particles around them float. That is what the equivalence principle promises.

But only **approximately**. Look at the four highlighted particles:

- Two particles lying **side by side** in the horizontal direction (blue) both fall toward the **center** of the planet. Their two paths converge, so the two particles **move closer together**.
- Two particles lying **one above the other** along the radial direction (pink): the one nearer the planet is pulled harder than the one farther away (gravity falls off as $1/r^2$), so they **move apart**.

The faint trail behind each particle is the path it has traveled. At first the trails are parallel; later they converge (the horizontal pair) or spread apart (the vertical pair).

> [Thử ngay] Drag the yellow dot (the release point) closer to or farther from the planet and let go: the cloud falls again from the new spot. The closer you release it, the faster the two pairs of particles separate and converge. Hover over the planet to see its data.
> [[Release again|tha]] [[Camera follows the cloud|theo]] [[Full view|toan]]

The difference in gravity between two nearby places is called the {{lực thủy triều|tidal force}}. No way of falling can remove it, because two particles at two different places “need” two different ways of falling.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.2.ten: A sphere becomes an egg: stretch 2GM/r³, squeeze GM/r³
bai.baiGiang.buoc.2.noiDung:
Now look at the whole cloud. The sphere of particles turns into an **ellipsoid** (an elongated egg shape): longer along the direction toward the planet, squeezed in the two sideways directions. The wireframe is the ellipsoid fitted to the cloud, recomputed every frame along its three principal axes.

The arrows are the **relative acceleration** of each particle with respect to the center of the cloud: pointing **outward** at the two ends (pink), **inward** around the horizontal ring (blue). For a particle a small distance $\xi$ from the center of the cloud:

$$ \ddot\xi_{\text{along}} = +\frac{2GM}{r^3}\,\xi_{\text{along}} $$

$$ \ddot\xi_{\text{across}} = -\frac{GM}{r^3}\,\xi_{\text{across}} $$

$G$ is the gravitational constant, $M$ the mass of the planet, $r$ the distance from the planet’s center to the cloud. Stretch $2GM/r^3$ along the radial direction, squeeze $GM/r^3$ in each sideways direction: **the three numbers add up to zero**. However much the cloud lengthens, it narrows by the same amount, and at first its volume stays the same.

> [Ví dụ] Aboard the International Space Station ($r = 6\,771$ km), two water droplets 1 m apart vertically have a relative acceleration $2GM/r^3 = 2{,}6 \times 10^{-6}$ m/s². Tiny, but it adds up: after about ten minutes the two droplets are roughly half a meter farther apart (a rough estimate, ignoring the station’s motion around Earth).

> [Thử ngay] [[Release again|tha]] [[Follow the cloud|theo]] [[Show or hide arrows|mui]]

> [Lưu ý] **Sound**: two sustained notes both start at 330 Hz at release. The glassy note follows the radial axis, the soft note follows the sideways axis; frequency is proportional to the axis length, so an axis twice as long sounds exactly one octave higher. The more the cloud deforms, the farther apart the two notes drift. This is a translation for the ear, not a real sound.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.2.thuThach.de: Drag the release point and let go so that **exactly at t = 3** (the clock in the readout), the radial axis of the ellipsoid is **one and a half times** as long as at release: 1.50 ± 0.05.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.2.thuThach.goiY: At first the radial axis grows like $1 + (GM/r^3)\,t^2$, so to get 1.5 at $t = 3$ you need $GM/r^3$ to be about 0.06. The cloud also falls closer and gets stretched harder and harder: try releasing between r = 8 and 9 and adjust from there. Turn off “Camera follows the cloud” to make dragging easier.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.3.noiDung:
Each freely falling particle follows a {{đường trắc địa|geodesic}} of spacetime (Lesson 10). Two neighboring particles start at rest relative to each other: their two geodesics start out **parallel**. In flat spacetime, two parallel straight lines keep their distance forever. Here they do not: the horizontal pair converges, the vertical pair spreads apart. That is exactly the sign of **{{độ cong|curvature}}**, like two meridians that are parallel at the equator but meet at the North Pole.

General relativity writes this as the **geodesic deviation equation**:

$$ \frac{\dd^2 \xi^i}{\dd \tau^2} = -R^i_{\ 0j0}\,\xi^j $$

$\xi$ is the vector joining two nearby particles, $\tau$ is proper time, and $R$ is the **Riemann tensor**, the thing that measures curvature. Compare with the previous step: $-R^i_{\ 0j0}$ is exactly the stretch-and-squeeze matrix (stretch $2GM/r^3$, squeeze $GM/r^3$).

> [Hiểu sai thường gặp] “Switch to a freely falling frame and every gravitational effect disappears.” Only the **uniform** part disappears (Lesson 8). The **difference** between two points cannot be removed by any frame. Uniform gravity in an elevator is just a matter of choosing a frame; curvature is real.

+++ Go deeper: from Newton to the tidal tensor
The acceleration of a particle at position $\vec r$ is $\vec a = -GM\vec r/r^3$. A neighboring particle at $\vec r + \vec\xi$ has acceleration $\vec a(\vec r + \vec\xi) \approx \vec a(\vec r) + (\xi \cdot \nabla)\vec a$. The difference of the two accelerations is

$$ \ddot\xi_i = T_{ij}\,\xi_j $$

$$ T_{ij} = \frac{\partial a_i}{\partial x_j} = \frac{GM}{r^5}\big(3x_ix_j - r^2\delta_{ij}\big) $$

Take the $x$ axis along the radial direction ($\vec r = (r;\ 0;\ 0)$): $T = \tfrac{GM}{r^3}\,\mathrm{diag}(2;\ -1;\ -1)$. The diagonal elements add up to 0, because $\nabla \cdot \vec a = -4\pi G\rho = 0$ outside matter.

In general relativity, for someone falling freely along the radial direction around a Schwarzschild black hole, the curvature components measured in that person’s frame give exactly $\mathrm{diag}(2;\ -1;\ -1)\,GM/r^3$, even right at the horizon. Hartle (2003), chapter 21, treats geodesic deviation and the Riemann tensor in more detail. The Newtonian mechanics used in the model departs from Einstein’s geodesics only by about $GM/(rc^2)$, which is very small for a planet.
+++
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.ten: Volume: outside matter and inside matter
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.noiDung:
The graph below the control panel tracks three quantities over time: the radial axis of the ellipsoid (pink), the sideways axis (blue) and the volume (yellow), all relative to their values at release. The dashed lines are the second-order prediction:

$$ \frac{a_{\text{along}}}{a_0} = 1 + \frac{GM}{r^3}t^2, \qquad \frac{a_{\text{across}}}{a_0} = 1 - \frac{GM}{2r^3}t^2 $$

$$ \frac{V}{V_0} = \frac{a_{\text{along}}}{a_0}\Big(\frac{a_{\text{across}}}{a_0}\Big)^2 = 1 + (\text{order } t^4) $$

**Outside matter**, the volume at first does not change: the yellow line stays flat for a while and only later departs (once the cloud has fallen close to the planet and is strongly deformed).

Now put the cloud **inside** a ball of matter of uniform density $\rho$ (like a tunnel through a planet, or a large cloud of dust). Inside, the acceleration is proportional to the distance from the center: $\vec a = -\tfrac{4\pi G\rho}{3}\vec r$. Every direction is squeezed equally, and the volume **shrinks right from the start**:

$$ \frac{\ddot V}{V} = -4\pi G\rho $$

> [Thử ngay] In the inside-matter mode, drag the yellow dot completely outside the ball and let go: the yellow line on the graph is flat at first again, because there is no matter there.
> [[Outside matter|ngoai]] [[Inside matter|trong]]

> [Lưu ý] In a uniform ball, every particle released from rest reaches the center **at the same moment**, so the cloud shrinks to a point and then expands on the other side. The tunnel and the transparent matter are only there so you can see; the particles collide with nothing.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.thuThach.de: Press “Inside matter,” then drag the release point **completely outside** the ball of matter and let go. You succeed when at t = 1.5 the volume is still at least **0.95** of its value at release (released inside, only about 0.57 is left).
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.thuThach.goiY: The ball of matter has radius 7.6 and the cloud has radius 1.1: the center of the cloud must be at least 8.7 from the center of the ball for the whole cloud to lie outside the matter. There, V̈/V at release is 0.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.5.noiDung:
Baez and Bunn (2005) showed that the whole of {{phương trình Einstein|Einstein’s equation}} can be summed up in one sentence about this very cloud:

> [Định nghĩa] Take a small ball of freely falling particles, initially at rest relative to one another. Its volume $V$ starts to shrink with an acceleration proportional to the **energy density plus three times the pressure** there:
> $$ \frac{\ddot V}{V}\Big|_{t=0} = -4\pi G\left(\rho + \frac{3P}{c^2}\right) $$

$\rho$ is the mass density (energy divided by $c^2$), $P$ is the pressure. Outside matter both are 0: the volume at first does not change (step 4). For cold dust, $P \approx 0$: you get exactly $-4\pi G\rho$. Pressure also **gravitates**, something Newton’s theory does not have.

The full form is a tensor equation:

$$ G_{\mu\nu} + \Lambda g_{\mu\nu} = \frac{8\pi G}{c^4}\,T_{\mu\nu} $$

- $g_{\mu\nu}$: the {{metric|metric}}, which tells how to measure distances and times.
- $G_{\mu\nu}$: the Einstein tensor, built from the curvature (the Riemann tensor) of the metric. The part of the curvature that tells whether a volume shrinks or grows is called the Ricci tensor; the “volume shrinks” statement above is exactly one of its components.
- $T_{\mu\nu}$: the {{tenxơ năng-xung lượng|stress–energy tensor}}: energy density, energy flow, pressure, stress.
- $\Lambda$: the {{hằng số vũ trụ|cosmological constant}}.
- $\mu, \nu$ run over 0, 1, 2, 3; both tensors are symmetric, so there are **10 equations**.

Wheeler summed it up: matter tells spacetime how to curve; spacetime tells matter how to move.

> [Thử ngay] [[Inside matter|trong]] [[Outside matter|ngoai]]
bai.baiGiang.buoc.6.noiDung:
The same sentence, “the volume shrinks according to $\rho + 3P/c^2$,” yields three very different phenomena:

1. **Tides.** Outside matter, the cloud keeps its volume but is stretched: the Moon pulls the layer of water around Earth into **two bulges**, one facing the Moon and one on the opposite side. Earth turns once beneath these two bulges every 24 hours 50 minutes, so each place has **two high tides** a day.
2. **Gravitational collapse.** For particles falling freely through ordinary matter ($\rho > 0$, $P \ge 0$), the volume always shrinks: clouds of dust and gas contract by themselves. A star holds itself up because pressure differences push the matter outward, meaning the matter inside a star is not in free fall. But pressure also contributes to gravity, so when a star is compressed too far (Lesson 11), more pressure only makes gravity stronger, and the star collapses into a black hole (Lesson 15).
3. **Accelerating expansion.** If the pressure is **negative** enough, $P \lt -\rho c^2/3$, then $\rho + 3P/c^2 \lt 0$ and the volume **expands faster and faster**. Dark energy (the cosmological constant) has $P = -\rho c^2$, which satisfies this condition: a relative acceleration $+\tfrac{\Lambda c^2}{3}\vec r$ pushes every particle away from every other. Lesson 18 applies exactly this to the whole universe.

> [Thử ngay] In tide mode, drag the Moon around Earth: the two water bulges turn with it. Drag it farther away: the bulges shrink very quickly, because the tidal force falls off as $1/d^3$. The sound of waves at the city gets louder as the water rises and quieter as it ebbs (illustrative sound).
> [[Tides on Earth|trieu]] [[Collapse: inside matter|trong]] [[Dark energy|toi]]

> [Lưu ý] In tide mode the water bulges are **exaggerated about 2 million times** (the real bulge crest is only about 0.36 m above mean sea level, on a radius of 6,371 km), and the Moon has been pulled about 15 times closer to fit the frame. This is the idealized “equilibrium” tide; real coastlines are also affected by the sea floor and the continents.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.6.thuThach.de: In tide mode, drag the Moon away until the crest of the water bulge is only **half** of today’s: 0.18 ± 0.01 m (see the readout).
bai.baiGiang.buoc.6.thuThach.goiY: The bulge height is proportional to $1/d^3$. To get half, $d^3$ must double, so $d$ must grow by a factor of $\sqrt[3]{2} \approx 1{,}26$: about 12.6 in the picture.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.7.ten: The numbers: from the ocean to black holes
bai.baiGiang.buoc.7.noiDung:
The tidal stretch along the radial direction is $2GM/r^3$ for each meter. Plugging in:

| Where | Calculation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| The Moon pulling water on Earth | $2GM_{\text{Moon}}R/d^3$ | $1{,}1 \times 10^{-6}$ m/s² |
| International Space Station, per meter | $2GM_{\text{Earth}}/r^3$, $r = 6\,771$ km | $2{,}6 \times 10^{-6}$ m/s² |
| Horizon of a 10-solar-mass black hole, 2 m tall person | $c^2 \times 2\,\text{m}/r_s^2$ | about $2 \times 10^{8}$ m/s² |
| Horizon of Sgr A* (4.3 million solar masses), 2 m tall person | same as above | about $10^{-3}$ m/s² |

($GM_{\text{Moon}} = 4{,}9028 \times 10^{12}$ m³/s², $R = 6\,371$ km, $d = 384\,400$ km.)

At the horizon $r = r_s = 2GM/c^2$, so $2GM/r_s^3 = c^2/r_s^2$: the **smaller** the black hole, the **stronger** the tide at its horizon. A 10-solar-mass black hole has $r_s \approx 30$ km; a difference of two hundred million m/s² between head and feet would stretch a person into spaghetti long before reaching the horizon. Sgr A* has $r_s \approx 1{,}3 \times 10^{7}$ km: the difference is only a thousandth of a m/s², less than the jolt of an elevator. You could cross the horizon of a giant black hole and **feel nothing**.

> [Thử ngay] [[Tides on Earth|trieu]] [[Falling toward the planet|ngoai]]
bai.baiGiang.buoc.7.thuThach.de: Drag the release point closer to the planet so that the stretch $2GM/r^3$ at release is **8 times** that at the default release point r = 11 (8 ± 0.6; see the “Release point” line in the readout).
bai.baiGiang.buoc.7.thuThach.goiY: The stretch goes as $1/r^3$: 8 times means $r$ is halved, $r \approx 5{,}5$. Turn off “Camera follows the cloud” to make dragging easier.
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.1.ten: Relative acceleration outside a spherical mass
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.1.y: Stretch along the radial direction, squeeze in the two sideways directions; the three coefficients add up to 0.
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.2.y: $R$ is the Riemann tensor (curvature). Outside a spherical mass, in a freely falling frame: $-R^i_{\ 0j0} = \frac{GM}{r^3}\,\mathrm{diag}(2;\ -1;\ -1)$.
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.3.ten: Einstein’s equation in words (Baez and Bunn 2005)
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.3.y: A small ball of freely falling particles, initially at rest relative to one another. With a cosmological constant, add $\Lambda c^2$ to the right-hand side.
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.5.y: The smaller the black hole, the stronger the tide at its horizon.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.hoi: An astronaut in free fall feels no gravity. What remains, no matter how the astronaut falls?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.chon.2: The tidal force: objects at two nearby places still have a relative acceleration
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.giai: Free fall removes the uniform part of gravity at one place. The difference between two different places (the tidal force) cannot be removed by any frame; it is the curvature of spacetime itself.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.hoi: A cloud of particles falling toward a planet is stretched along the radial direction with coefficient 2GM/r³. In each sideways direction, it is squeezed with what coefficient?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.giai: Outside matter, the three coefficients add up to 0 (the tidal tensor is traceless): 2 − 1 − 1 = 0. Picking GM/(2r³) confuses it with the coefficient in the semi-axis formula $1 - GMt^2/(2r^3)$, which has an extra factor ½ from integrating twice.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.hoi: A small ball of dust particles at rest relative to one another, outside all matter, starts to fall freely. At first its volume:
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.chon.3: Stays the same (its acceleration is 0), even though its shape becomes an ellipsoid
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.giai: Einstein’s equation with $\rho = P = 0$ gives $\ddot V/V = 0$. The cloud lengthens in one direction and narrows in the other two by exactly compensating amounts. Only where there is matter ($\rho > 0$) does the volume shrink right from the start.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.hoi: Why does dark energy make the universe expand faster and faster?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.chon.2: Because its pressure is negative and large enough: P = −ρc² is less than −ρc²/3, so ρ + 3P/c² < 0
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.chon.3: Because it pushes galaxies with a new force
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.giai: With $P = -\rho c^2$: $\rho + 3P/c^2 = -2\rho \lt 0$, so $\ddot V/V = +8\pi G\rho > 0$: the volume grows faster and faster. Its energy density is still positive; it is the negative pressure that flips the sign.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.hoi: Which black hole is more dangerous for someone falling through the horizon: a 10-solar-mass black hole or Sgr A* (4.3 million solar masses)?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.chon.1: Sgr A*, because it is heavier
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.chon.2: The 10-solar-mass black hole, because the tide at the horizon goes as c²/rs², and a small black hole has a small rs
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.chon.3: They are the same, because every horizon is alike
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.giai: At the horizon $2GM/r_s^3 = c^2/r_s^2$. For 10 solar masses, the difference for a 2 m tall person is about $2 \times 10^8$ m/s²; for Sgr A* it is only about $10^{-3}$ m/s².
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.6.hoi: Why are there two high tides a day rather than one?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.6.dap: The tidal force stretches the layer of water along the Earth–Moon line toward BOTH sides: the side facing the Moon is pulled harder than Earth’s center, the far side is pulled less hard than Earth’s center, so both sides “fall behind” relative to the center, forming two symmetric bulges. Earth turns once beneath those two bulges in about 24 hours 50 minutes, so each place passes under both bulges, giving two high tides about 12 hours 25 minutes apart.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.1: J. C. Baez and E. F. Bunn, “The Meaning of Einstein’s Equation,” Am. J. Phys. 73, 644 (2005): Einstein’s equation stated in terms of the volume of a ball of freely falling particles.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.2: J. B. Hartle, *Gravity: An Introduction to Einstein’s General Relativity* (2003), chapter 21: curvature, geodesic deviation, Einstein’s equation.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.3: C. W. Misner, K. S. Thorne and J. A. Wheeler, *Gravitation* (1973): tidal forces and curvature.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.4: K. S. Thorne, *Black Holes and Time Warps* (1994): tides around black holes, “spaghettification.”
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.1.nghia: The change in distance between two nearby geodesics. In curved spacetime, two lines that start out parallel will converge or spread apart; the geodesic deviation equation links this to the Riemann tensor.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.2.nghia: The quantity that fully measures the curvature of spacetime at a point; in a freely falling frame, part of it is exactly the matrix of tidal accelerations.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.3.nghia: The matrix that gives the relative acceleration of two nearby particles in terms of the vector joining them. Outside a spherical mass: stretch 2GM/r³ along the radial direction, squeeze GM/r³ in each sideways direction.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.4.nghia: The combination of curvature (from the Riemann tensor) on the left-hand side of Einstein’s equation.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.5.nghia: The shape the water layer would take if Earth were entirely covered by water and the water had time to flow with the tidal force: two symmetric bulges, with a height difference of about half a meter due to the Moon.
